def: The repeating cycle in which an application sends the conversation and the tool definitions to the model, runs whatever tools the model asks for, appends the outputs to the history, and calls the model again until a reply arrives that requests no more tools.
eg: Claude never runs your tools itself: your code or the Agent SDK drives this cycle. The exam asks what makes it continue and what makes it stop.

def: The field on every Messages API response that states why generation ended: the model finished, asked for a tool, ran into the output limit, and so on. Loop code branches on this value rather than on the wording of the reply.
eg: The correct loop is keyed on this field. Parsing the prose of the reply is the classic wrong answer.

def: The value showing that the model has requested one or more tool calls and is waiting for their results. The application must run the tools, append the results to the history, and call the model again.
eg: Each request arrives as a content block with an id, a tool name and an input object that matches the tool schema.

def: The value showing that the model finished its reply naturally and requested no tools. It is the normal signal to leave the loop and present the answer.
eg: Other values still need handling: hitting the output limit, a refusal, and a paused server-tool turn.

def: The value showing that the reply was cut off by the output-token limit. If the cut-off text ends in a half-written tool request, repeat the call with a larger limit instead of executing the fragment.
eg: A truncated tool request has incomplete input, so running it would be a bug.

def: The content block, sent in a user message, that carries a tool's output back to the model. It names the request it answers by id, may flag a failure, and must come before any plain text in that message.
eg: Every tool request needs exactly one matching result in the very next user message. Misordered blocks are a common cause of 400 errors.

def: A property of the service: it keeps no memory between requests, so the application resends the whole message list, including the model's earlier tool requests and the results it returned, on every call.
eg: This is how new tool results reach the next reasoning step: they are appended to the history that is sent again.

def: Letting the model reason from the current context and the latest tool results about which tool to call next, or whether to stop, instead of following a script written in advance.
eg: This adaptivity is what makes a system an agent. It is also why hard guarantees need code rather than prompt wording.

def: A hard-coded flow of branches and tool sequences written by the developer in advance. It is predictable and easy to test, but it cannot react to what an intermediate result reveals.
eg: Choose it when the steps are really known up front; choose model-driven control when they depend on what is found.

def: An anti-pattern that ends the loop when the model's prose contains a phrase such as "all done". Wording varies from run to run, so the loop either stops too early or never stops.
eg: The structured stop signal on the response is the reliable test.

term: Iteration cap as the primary stop
def: An anti-pattern that ends the loop when a counter reaches a fixed number of rounds regardless of progress, cutting off unfinished work or hiding runaway behavior. Such a limit belongs only as a safety net.
eg: Turn and budget limits are legitimate guardrails, but hitting one produces an error result, not a finished answer.

def: An anti-pattern that treats the presence of assistant text in a response as proof that the task is finished. Models routinely write text next to a tool request in the same turn.
eg: A reply with text and a pending tool request is not finished. Check the stop signal, not whether words exist.

def: Several tool requests emitted in a single model response. The application may run independent, side-effect-free ones concurrently, and it returns every result together in the next user message.
eg: In the Agent SDK read-only tools can run concurrently while Edit, Write and Bash run one at a time. Dependent calls belong in later turns.

def: The field on the Agent SDK's final message that says whether the run finished successfully or stopped on a limit or an error, for example the turn cap or the spending cap.
eg: Check it before reading the result text: only the success variant carries a final answer. Limit variants include error_max_turns and error_max_budget_usd.

def: An SDK option that limits the number of tool-use round trips in a run; a sibling option caps estimated spend. Reaching either ends the run with an error result subtype.
eg: Treat these as production guardrails, not as the way a healthy agent normally finishes.

def: A workflow of fixed, sequential model calls in which each step works on the previous step's output and the order never changes. It suits predictable, multi-aspect work such as analyzing each file and then running one cross-file pass.
eg: It trades flexibility for predictability and easy testing. Contrast it with dynamic decomposition for open-ended investigation.

def: Planning an open-ended task by generating and reprioritizing subtasks from what each earlier step discovers, instead of following a list fixed in advance.
eg: Use it for investigation and legacy-code work where the next step depends on what was just found.

def: The drop in review quality when too many items are examined in one pass: depth becomes uneven, obvious problems are missed, and judgments about the same pattern contradict each other.
eg: A bigger context window does not by itself cure it. Splitting the work into focused passes does.

def: A review design that analyzes each changed file on its own for local defects, then runs a separate pass aimed at data flow and contracts between the files.
eg: It is prompt chaining applied to code review, and the standard fix for inconsistent single-pass reviews of large changes.

def: An approach for open-ended work such as adding tests to a legacy codebase: first map the structure, then find the highest-impact areas, then follow a prioritized plan that is revised as dependencies surface.
eg: It is dynamic decomposition applied to a concrete task, and the opposite of a fixed checklist written before looking at the code.

def: The library that embeds Claude Code's autonomous loop, built-in tools, hooks, subagents and session handling in your own application, so you configure an agent instead of writing the loop by hand.
eg: It streams messages while the loop runs and ends with a final result message that carries the session id, cost and outcome.

def: A star-shaped multi-agent topology in which every message between specialists passes through one central node. Specialists connect only to that node, never to each other, so logging, error handling and information flow are managed in one place.
eg: The single hub is what makes the system observable and controllable. Peer-to-peer chatter between specialists is the anti-pattern.

def: The agent that receives the request, breaks it into subtasks, chooses which specialists to call, aggregates what they return, and judges whether coverage is good enough or more work is needed.
eg: When a final report has gaps but every specialist did its job, suspect the decomposition performed here.

def: A separate agent instance launched by another agent to handle a focused subtask, with its own context window, instructions and tool set. Only its final message returns to the agent that launched it.
eg: Subagents keep exploration noise out of the parent's context and can run in parallel.

def: The property that a spawned agent begins with a fresh conversation: it cannot see the parent's history, earlier tool results or other subagents' work, so everything it needs must be written into its prompt.
eg: The commonest multi-agent bug is a subagent asked to "summarize the findings" that were never actually passed to it.

def: The built-in tool a coordinator calls to start a subagent, supplying a prompt and a subagent type. The coordinator must be permitted to use it, and several calls in one response run in parallel. The exam guide and older SDKs use its former name.
eg: Current documentation calls it Agent and still accepts Task as an alias, so treat the two names as the same mechanism.

def: The configuration object for a subagent type: a description that tells the coordinator when to use it, a system prompt that defines its behavior, and optional settings such as an allowed-tool list and a model.
eg: The tool list is where least privilege is enforced for each specialist.

def: An SDK option that pre-approves the listed tools so they run without a permission prompt. A coordinator is configured with the subagent-spawning tool in this list (named Task in the exam guide, Agent in current docs).
eg: It is a permission setting. The set of tools a subagent can see is controlled by the tools field of its definition.

def: Writing the findings, file paths, constraints and earlier results that a subagent needs directly into its delegation prompt, because it has no other way to see them.
eg: Include complete prior outputs, not a vague pointer such as "use what the search agent found".

def: Emitting several subagent-launching calls in a single coordinator response so independent specialists run at the same time; total latency approaches the slowest task rather than the sum of all of them.
eg: Calls placed in separate turns run one after another, which is the sequential-where-parallel-was-possible mistake.

def: An anti-pattern of launching subagents whose work does not depend on each other across separate coordinator turns, so the total time becomes the sum of their durations.
eg: Sequence only genuine dependencies, such as synthesis needing search results first.

def: A coordinator failure in which the subtasks it creates cover only part of a broad topic, so every subagent succeeds at its assignment yet the final output has large gaps.
eg: Diagnose it by reading the coordinator's subtask list before blaming the downstream agents.

def: Having the coordinator analyze each query and invoke only the specialists it needs, instead of always pushing every request through the full pipeline.
eg: A simple factual lookup should not trigger search, analysis, synthesis and report agents.

def: Assigning each subagent a distinct subtopic, source type or time range so that their work does not overlap and together they cover the question.
eg: Without it, parallel agents tend to retrieve the same popular sources and miss the rest.

def: A coordinator cycle in which it examines the synthesized output for gaps, sends targeted follow-up queries to the search and analysis agents, and re-runs synthesis until coverage is sufficient.
eg: It turns a one-shot pipeline into a self-correcting one. Stop on a coverage criterion, not on a blind round count.

def: Writing coordinator instructions that state the research goal and the quality bar and leave the method to the subagent, rather than dictating step-by-step procedures.
eg: Rigid procedures stop subagents from adapting when a source turns out to be unavailable or unhelpful.

def: Passing findings between agents as structured records in which the substance is kept apart from details such as source URL, document name, page number and date, so attribution survives each hand-off.
eg: Free-form prose summaries are where citations quietly disappear.

def: An anti-pattern in which several subagents read and write one common conversation or scratch state. Results become order-dependent, authorship is unclear, and the isolation that makes subagents useful is lost.
eg: Give each agent its own context and merge results explicitly in the coordinator.

def: The coordinator step that combines the specialists' outputs, reconciles overlaps and conflicts, and decides whether to re-delegate before handing off to synthesis or the final report.
eg: Aggregation is a coordinator duty. Subagents should not need to know about each other.

def: A specialist that merges gathered findings into one coherent, attributed output. It works from what it is given and should not need broad search tools.
eg: If it keeps trying to search, either its tool set is too wide or the findings it received were incomplete.

def: The coordinator decides which subagent to invoke by reading each definition's description, so vague or overlapping descriptions cause work to be sent to the wrong specialist.
eg: Treat these descriptions like tool descriptions: say what the agent is for and what it is not for.

def: The rule on the way back from a subagent: its intermediate tool calls and results never reach the parent, and only its closing message is delivered, which keeps the parent's context small.
eg: Ask for a concise, structured closing report, because that message is all the coordinator gets.

def: Choosing how many subagents and tool calls to spend according to how hard the query is: a simple lookup gets one agent and a few calls, while broad research may fan out to several specialists.
eg: Over-delegating on trivial questions wastes tokens and time, and under-delegating on broad ones loses coverage.

def: An anti-pattern in which specialists exchange messages directly with one another, bypassing the coordinator, which makes failures hard to trace and information flow hard to control.
eg: The exam prefers routing everything through the coordinator for observability and consistent error handling.

def: A coordinator failure in which a subagent receives a short, underspecified task, so agents duplicate each other's work, leave gaps, or research the wrong period or subject.
eg: A good delegation prompt names the objective, the boundaries, the output format and the tools or sources to favor.

def: Controls implemented in code, such as gates, hooks and validators, that the model cannot skip. They give deterministic compliance for rules where even one violation has serious consequences.
eg: The exam default for identity checks, payment limits and the ordering of financial operations.

def: Instructions, rules and examples placed in the system prompt that steer the model probabilistically. Even emphatic wording leaves a small but non-zero chance that a step is skipped or a rule broken.
eg: Good for style and judgment, but insufficient when one violation means a wrong refund or leaked data.

def: Code that blocks a downstream tool call until an upstream step has returned what it needs, for example refusing every refund request until customer lookup has produced a verified customer id.
eg: It enforces order, which few-shot examples and tool filtering cannot.

def: A callback that runs in the application at defined points of the agent loop, such as before or after a tool call, when a subagent stops, or before compaction, and can log, modify, block or add context.
eg: Hooks are the deterministic control surface of an agent: they run whether or not the model cooperates.

def: A hook that fires before a tool executes. It can allow, deny, ask about or rewrite the call; a denial prevents execution and the reason is returned to the model.
eg: Use it to enforce policy before an irreversible action, such as a payment, takes place.

def: A hook that fires after a tool returns. It can add context or replace the result before the model reads it, which makes it the place to clean up or standardize data.
eg: It cannot undo a side effect that already happened. Use the pre-execution hook to prevent one.

def: The field a pre-execution hook returns to allow, deny, ask or defer a tool call, with an optional reason shown to the model. When several hooks answer differently, the most restrictive answer wins.
eg: Put a reason in the denial so the model can pick another path instead of retrying blindly.

def: A pre-execution hook output that rewrites the arguments of a pending tool call, for example redirecting a file path into a sandbox. It is usually paired with an allow decision.
eg: Return a fresh object instead of mutating the original input, and place it inside the hook-specific output.

def: The rule that when hooks and permission rules disagree, a deny beats a defer, which beats an ask, which beats an allow. A single deny blocks the call regardless of what other hooks return.
eg: It lets you stack independent safety hooks without worrying about their order, because hooks for one event run in parallel.

def: A pattern, such as a tool name, a pipe-separated list of names, or a regular expression covering every tool of one MCP server, that decides which events trigger a hook. It matches tool names, not arguments such as file paths.
eg: To act on a path or an amount, inspect the tool input inside the callback.

def: Using a post-execution hook to convert inconsistent tool outputs, such as Unix timestamps, ISO 8601 strings and numeric status codes, into one format before the model reasons over them.
eg: It fixes the mismatch deterministically instead of hoping the prompt explains every format.

def: A pre-execution hook that blocks a tool call exceeding a business limit, such as a refund above a set amount, and returns a reason that steers the agent toward a human escalation workflow.
eg: The agent is redirected, not left stuck: the denial message should name the alternative path.

def: The fact that hooks execute in the application's own process, so they consume no context tokens and cannot be argued out of a decision, unlike instructions placed in the prompt.
eg: Another reason hooks, not prompt text, carry the rules that must always hold.

def: A compact record given to a human agent at escalation: customer identity, root cause, amounts involved, actions already taken and a recommended next step. The human cannot see the transcript, so the record must stand alone.
eg: Forwarding the raw conversation is the weaker answer. Distill what the human needs to act.

def: Splitting a message that contains several issues into distinct items, investigating them in parallel against shared customer context, and merging the findings into one coherent resolution.
eg: Handling the concerns one at a time and replying separately gives a disjointed experience and wastes time.

def: Transferring a case to a human partway through resolution, for example when a policy blocks the requested action. It only works well with a complete handoff summary, because the human starts without the conversation.
eg: The escalation tool's input should require the fields a human needs, so a thin handoff cannot be produced.

def: A hook that fires when a subagent finishes, used to log its outcome or to aggregate results from subagents that ran in parallel.
eg: Its sibling fires when a subagent starts, which helps track how many were spawned.

def: The saved conversation history of an agent run, including prompts, tool calls and results. It lets work be resumed later with full context, but it stores the conversation and not the state of files on disk.
eg: A resumed session remembers what was read, not whether the file has changed since.

def: Continuing a specific earlier Claude Code conversation by label, using claude --resume followed by the session name, after naming it at startup or with a rename command.
eg: Names make multi-day investigations resumable without hunting for ids.

def: Two ways back into a session: one automatically reopens the most recent session in the current directory, while the other targets a specific session by id or name.
eg: Pick the targeted form when several sessions exist, for example one per user or one per task.

def: An option that starts a new session as a copy of an existing session's history. The copy gets its own id, the original stays unchanged, and the two can then diverge.
eg: Forking branches the conversation only: file edits made in a fork are real and visible to every branch.

def: A completed exploration of a codebase that several forked sessions start from, so each can test a different approach, such as two testing strategies, without repeating the analysis.
eg: The expensive discovery work is paid once, and the experiments stay independent of each other.

def: Earlier file reads and command outputs sitting in a resumed conversation that no longer match the files on disk after edits, which can lead the agent to confident but wrong conclusions.
eg: The longer the gap and the more files changed, the less trustworthy the old results are.

def: Starting a new session and giving it a structured summary of verified findings instead of resuming a long history whose tool results are out of date. After large changes it is often the more reliable choice.
eg: The documentation itself notes that passing captured results into a fresh prompt can be more robust than shipping transcripts around.

def: When resuming after code was modified, telling the agent exactly which files changed so it re-reads only those, instead of assuming nothing changed or redoing the whole exploration.
eg: This is the middle path between trusting stale context and paying for a full restart.

def: What happens when one session is resumed in two places without forking: messages from both are written into a single transcript and the histories mix. Forking gives each place its own independent branch.
eg: If two people or terminals need to work from the same starting point, fork.

def: The natural-language text in a tool definition that the model reads to decide whether and how to call the tool. It is the primary signal for tool selection, so thin wording leads to unreliable choices between similar tools.
eg: Documentation advises several sentences per tool: purpose, when to use it and when not to, what each parameter means, and what it does not return.

def: The part of a description that says when to choose this tool instead of a similar one and what the tool does not do, so that close neighbors can be told apart.
eg: Two tools that both "look up" something need this line more than any other.

def: The JSON Schema object in a tool definition that declares the parameters the tool accepts, their types, which are required, and what each one means.
eg: Parameter descriptions inside the schema count as selection and formatting guidance too.

def: An optional list of example input objects in a tool definition that shows valid calls. It helps with nested or format-sensitive parameters, and every example must satisfy the schema.
eg: It supplements a good description. It does not replace one.

def: Two or more tools whose descriptions are nearly identical, so the model cannot tell them apart and routes requests unpredictably between them, as with two generic analyzers that both claim to "analyze content".
eg: Fix the descriptions or names first, before adding routing layers or examples.

def: Changing a tool's name and description to reflect a narrow purpose, for example turning a generic analyzer into one specifically for extracting web results, so that functional overlap disappears.
eg: A name is part of the description. A vague name keeps the confusion alive even if the text is improved.

def: Replacing one generic, overloaded tool with several tools that each have a defined purpose and input/output contract, such as separate tools to extract data points, summarize content and verify a claim against its source.
eg: Do this when one tool tries to serve different purposes with different outputs. Merging genuinely related operations is a different, also valid, design choice.

def: System prompt wording whose phrases accidentally associate a request type with the wrong tool, overriding the careful descriptions on the tools themselves.
eg: Review the system prompt whenever selection looks wrong despite good descriptions.

def: Prefixing tool names with the service or resource they belong to, such as github_list_prs, so that selection stays unambiguous as the number of tools grows.
eg: The same idea appears in MCP, where tool names are shown with the server name in front.

def: A tool-definition setting that constrains the model's token sampling so that tool inputs always match the schema, eliminating missing fields and wrong types. It does not guarantee that the values themselves are sensible.
eg: It removes syntax-level failures, not semantic ones such as a refund amount that is the wrong number.

def: The boolean in an MCP tool result that marks the call as failed. The failure travels back as an ordinary result the model can read and react to, instead of crashing the run.
eg: Without it, an error message looks like valid data and the agent may build on it.

term: Tool execution error versus protocol error
def: MCP separates failures the model can act on, such as a rejected input or a business rule, which come back inside the tool result, from request-level faults such as an unknown tool, which come back as JSON-RPC errors.
eg: Execution errors are written for the model to self-correct. Protocol errors are less likely to be recoverable by the model.

def: A temporary failure, such as a timeout or a briefly unavailable service, that may succeed if the same call is repeated after a short wait.
eg: The only category where automatic retry with backoff is the right first move.

def: A failure because the input was malformed, missing or out of range. Repeating the identical call will fail again, so the model should correct the input.
eg: The message should say which field was wrong and what a valid value looks like.

def: A failure because a rule or policy forbids the action, such as a refund requested outside the allowed window. It is not retryable and calls for a customer-friendly explanation or an escalation.
eg: Flag it as non-retryable and supply wording the agent can pass on to the customer.

def: A failure because the caller is not authorized for the resource or action. Retrying cannot help, so the agent needs different access or a human.
eg: Do not blur it with a transient fault: a retry loop here only burns time.

def: The distinction that tells an agent whether repeating a call could succeed. Returning it as structured metadata prevents wasted retry attempts on failures that can never succeed.
eg: Pair it with the error category so the agent knows what to do instead.

def: A consistent error payload carried in the tool result, typically a category, a retryable flag and a human-readable description, so the agent can choose between retrying, rephrasing, explaining or escalating.
eg: The category and retryable fields are an application convention; the protocol itself defines only the failure flag.

def: An anti-pattern of returning one vague message, such as "Operation failed", for every kind of failure, which leaves the agent unable to choose a sensible recovery.
eg: The exam contrasts it with categorized, structured errors.

def: A subagent retrying transient failures itself and passing up to the coordinator only what it cannot resolve, together with what it tried and any partial results.
eg: It keeps routine blips out of the coordinator's way while still reporting real failures with context.

def: The difference between a query that could not be completed, such as a timeout, which may need a retry decision, and one that ran successfully and found nothing, which is a valid answer.
eg: Reporting an outage as "no results" is silent error suppression and misleads every agent downstream.

def: Giving one agent a very long tool list, for example eighteen tools instead of four or five, which raises decision complexity and makes wrong selections more likely.
eg: The usual cure is to split the work across specialized agents with small, relevant tool sets.

def: Giving each agent only the tools its role requires, plus at most a few narrow cross-role tools for frequent needs. It improves selection reliability and prevents out-of-role actions.
eg: Least privilege applied to tools.

def: An agent using tools outside its specialty, such as a synthesis agent attempting web searches, because those tools sit in its tool set.
eg: Remove the temptation rather than writing "do not search" in the prompt.

def: A deliberately narrow tool given to one agent to cover a frequent need, such as a simple fact-checking lookup for the synthesis agent, while rare complex cases still go through the coordinator.
eg: It cuts round trips for the common case without giving the agent a whole foreign toolbox.

def: Swapping a powerful generic tool for a narrower one with validation, for example replacing a fetch-any-URL tool with a document loader that checks the address is a valid document location.
eg: A tighter contract means fewer ways to misuse the tool.

def: The request parameter that controls whether and which tool the model must call. Its settings are automatic choice, require some tool, require one named tool, and no tools.
eg: Know what each setting guarantees: it decides whether plain text or a tool call can come back.

def: The default setting under which the model decides for itself whether to answer in text or to call one or more of the supplied tools.
eg: With this setting a plain-text reply is always possible, so it cannot guarantee that a tool is called.

def: The setting that requires the model to call one of the supplied tools rather than reply in plain text, while leaving the choice of which tool to the model.
eg: Fits cases such as several extraction schemas where the document type is unknown but a structured result is mandatory.

def: The setting that names one specific tool the model must call. It guarantees that a particular step, such as metadata extraction, runs first, with later steps handled in follow-up turns.
eg: The format is a type of "tool" plus the tool name.

term: No preamble under forced tool choice
def: Because requiring or forcing a tool prefills the start of the reply, the model emits the tool call without any natural-language explanation first, even when asked for one.
eg: To get explanation plus a tool call, use automatic choice and ask for it in the prompt.

def: Not every model or setting accepts the require-some-tool and require-one-tool modes: they are rejected with manual extended thinking and, per current documentation, on several of the newest models, where automatic choice plus strict tool use is the substitute.
eg: The exam tests what the modes guarantee. In practice, check the documentation for your model before relying on them.

def: An open protocol, built on JSON-RPC, that lets LLM applications connect to external servers which expose tools, resources and prompts in a standard way, so one integration works with many applications.
eg: Think of it as the standard socket between an agent and your backend systems.

def: The three roles of the architecture: the host application coordinates the model and creates one client per connection, and each server supplies capabilities while being unable to see the whole conversation or other servers.
eg: The isolation between servers is deliberate. The host controls what crosses between them.

def: Functions an MCP server exposes for the model to invoke, such as querying a database or creating a ticket. They are model-controlled and may have side effects.
eg: Use them for actions. Use resources for content the agent should be able to see.

def: Read-only content an MCP server exposes by URI, such as documents, database schemas or issue summaries, which the host application decides how to bring into context.
eg: The exam pairs them with the idea of reducing exploratory tool calls.

def: Reusable message templates that a server offers and the user selects explicitly, typically surfaced as slash commands.
eg: Tools are chosen by the model, resources by the application, prompts by the user.

def: A resource that lists what data exists, for example issue summaries, a documentation hierarchy or database schemas, so that an agent can see what is available without making exploratory tool calls.
eg: It answers "what do you have?" cheaply, before the agent decides what to fetch.

def: Server definitions stored in a .mcp.json file at the project root and committed to version control, so the whole team gets the same tooling. Claude Code asks for approval before first using them in an interactive session.
eg: The right home for shared team servers; never put secrets in it, use variable expansion.

def: Servers kept in your own ~/.claude.json that are available in all your projects but not shared with teammates, which suits personal or experimental tooling.
eg: If a teammate says they cannot see a server, check whether it was added at this scope instead of the project scope.

def: The default scope when adding a server from the command line: private to you and tied to the current project, stored in ~/.claude.json.
eg: Not to be confused with local settings files: this scope's data lives in the user-level JSON file.

def: When the same server name appears in several scopes, the whole entry from the highest-precedence source is used with no field-by-field merging; local beats project, which beats user.
eg: It explains why a personal override of a team server changes behavior only for you.

def: Variable syntax in the MCP configuration, such as ${GITHUB_TOKEN} or ${VAR:-default} (which supplies a fallback), that is replaced from the environment at load time, so secrets never have to be committed to the repository.
eg: It works in the command, arguments, env, url and headers fields.

def: The fact that tools from every configured MCP server are discovered when the session connects and are all available to the agent at once, whichever scope each server came from.
eg: This is why a shared server and a personal experimental one can be used side by side.

def: A default Claude Code behavior that loads only MCP tool names at the start of a session and fetches full tool definitions on demand, so adding servers costs little context.
eg: Without it, every server's full schemas would be sent on every request.

def: The form under which MCP tools appear in permission rules, hook matchers and allowed-tool lists; a wildcard can cover every tool from one server.
eg: The server part is the key you used when configuring it.

def: Guidance to adopt an existing, maintained server for standard integrations such as Jira or GitHub, and to build a custom server only for team-specific workflows that no existing server covers.
eg: Custom code is a maintenance burden. Save it for what is genuinely unique.

def: Writing a detailed description for an MCP tool, covering what it can do and what it returns, so that the agent chooses it over a weaker built-in alternative such as a plain text search.
eg: If the agent keeps reaching for the built-in tool, the MCP tool's description is usually too thin.

def: In the current specification, each request is self-contained and carries its own protocol version and capabilities, so a server cannot rely on per-connection state. Tools that need state return an explicit handle for later calls.
eg: The specification version dated 2026-07-28 describes this model.

def: The built-in tool that loads the full contents of a file into context, used to follow imports and trace flows once a search has located the right place.
eg: Pairs with a content search: search first to find the spot, read to understand it.

def: The built-in tool that creates a file or overwrites an existing one with the complete content supplied; it does not append or merge.
eg: It is also the fallback when a targeted edit cannot find a unique anchor: read the file, then write the updated whole.

def: The built-in tool that makes a targeted change by replacing an exact piece of existing text. The text to replace must match exactly and must occur only once in the file.
eg: It is cheaper and safer than rewriting a file, as long as a unique anchor exists.

def: The failure that occurs when the text chosen for a targeted replacement appears more than once in the file. Fix it by including more surrounding lines to make it unique, or by reading the file and writing the whole updated content.
eg: Repeating the same call changes nothing. Change the anchor or the method.

def: The built-in search for file contents: it finds lines matching a regular expression, such as every caller of a function, an error message or an import statement.
eg: In some Claude Code setups this search is done through the shell instead; the exam concept of content search is the same.

def: The built-in tool that finds files by path or name pattern, such as every file matching **/*.test.tsx, without looking inside them.
eg: Names and extensions go to this tool. Text inside files goes to content search.

def: The built-in tool that runs shell commands, scripts and version-control operations. It is powerful and has side effects, so it is the usual target of permission rules and hooks.
eg: Use the dedicated file tools when they fit, and the shell for everything else.

def: Building understanding in steps: search for entry points first, then read only the files needed to follow imports and trace the flow, instead of loading every file up front.
eg: It keeps context lean and keeps the agent focused on what matters for the question.

def: Finding where a function is really used when it is re-exported through wrapper modules: first list the exported names in each wrapper, then search the codebase for each of those names.
eg: Searching only for the original name misses callers that import it under a wrapper's name.

def: A markdown file of persistent instructions that Claude Code reads into context at the start of every session: build and test commands, conventions, architecture notes. It is guidance delivered as context, not enforced configuration.
eg: Treat it as what you would otherwise re-explain in every chat. Anything that must happen every time belongs in a hook or a permission rule instead.

def: The personal instruction file kept in the .claude folder of your home directory. It applies to you in every project on your machine, and because it lives outside any repository, teammates never receive it through version control.
eg: Classic diagnosis: a new teammate is missing the team's conventions because someone saved them here instead of in the project file.

def: The team-shared instruction file at the repository root, or inside the repository's .claude folder, that is committed to version control. Everyone who clones the project gets the same standards, commands and conventions.
eg: The right home for rules the whole team should follow; it loads for anyone who runs Claude Code in the project.

def: An instruction file placed in a subdirectory of the project. Claude Code loads it on demand, once Claude reads or edits a file in that directory, so it suits conventions that belong to one package or folder.
eg: It is bound to its own directory, which is why conventions that span many folders are better served by path-scoped rules.

def: A personal, project-specific instruction file at the project root that loads next to the shared one but is meant to stay out of version control. It holds things like your own sandbox URLs or preferred test data.
eg: Add it to .gitignore. At each directory level it is read after the shared file, so your notes come last.

def: An organization-wide instruction file that IT deploys to a fixed system location. It loads for every user on the machine and cannot be excluded by individual settings.
eg: Use it for company standards and compliance reminders. For technical enforcement, such as blocking commands, use managed settings rather than instructions.

def: How Claude Code combines instruction files: those in the working directory and every parent directory are loaded at launch and joined together rather than overriding one another, with files closer to the working directory read later.
eg: Contradictory instructions across files are not resolved by priority. Claude may follow either one, so keep the files consistent.

def: A way to pull another file into an instruction file by writing an at sign followed by its path. Relative paths resolve from the file that contains the import, nesting is allowed up to four hops, and the imported text loads at launch.
eg: It keeps a large setup modular, for example importing each package's standards, but it does not shrink context use because imported files load too.

def: A project folder of small markdown files, one topic each such as testing or API conventions, that Claude Code loads as instructions. It is the modular alternative to one monolithic instruction file.
eg: Files without a paths field load at launch like the main file; files with one load only when matching files are touched.

def: An anti-pattern: an instruction file stuffed with tutorials, file-by-file descriptions and rules that matter for one corner of the codebase. Past roughly two hundred lines it consumes context and the important rules get lost.
eg: Fixes: prune what Claude can derive from the code, move area-specific conventions into path-scoped rules, and move procedures into skills.

def: A feature in which Claude Code writes its own notes about your corrections and preferences into a per-project folder; the first 200 lines or 25 KB of its index file load each session. You can browse and edit the notes.
eg: Distinct from the instructions you write yourself, and machine-local: teammates do not receive it.

def: The built-in command that lists the instruction files in play across user and project scope, opens any of them for editing, and toggles auto memory.
eg: The exam uses it to diagnose inconsistent behavior across sessions. The context command additionally shows which memory files actually loaded at launch.

def: The built-in command that shows a live breakdown of what fills the context window, including the memory files that loaded at launch, with suggestions for heavy items.
eg: A subdirectory instruction file will not appear in its list at launch, because those load on demand.

def: The built-in command that analyzes the codebase and generates a starter instruction file with the build commands, test instructions and conventions it discovers. If one already exists, it suggests improvements instead of overwriting.
eg: Treat the output as a draft and add what Claude cannot discover by reading the code.

def: A command registered in a settings file that Claude Code runs at a lifecycle event, such as before or after a tool call. It gives deterministic behavior that instructions in a memory file cannot guarantee.
eg: A pre-tool hook that exits with code 2 blocks the call and feeds its message back to Claude, even in permission modes that skip prompts.

def: The order in which Claude Code resolves a setting defined in several places: organization-managed settings first, then command-line settings, then the project's local file, then the shared project file, then the user file. List settings such as allow rules merge instead of overriding.
eg: The local project file is the personal override that stays out of git; the shared project file is the one you commit.

def: A custom command defined as a markdown file in the repository's .claude/commands/ folder. Because it is committed, every developer gets it when they clone or pull.
eg: Current docs fold commands into skills: a command file and a skill directory with the same name both create the slash command, and the skill wins a clash.

def: A personal custom command stored under the .claude/commands/ folder in your home directory. It is available in all your projects but is never shared through version control.
eg: Choose it for private shortcuts. Team-wide commands belong in the project folder.

def: A folder under .claude/skills/ whose SKILL.md file combines YAML frontmatter and instructions for a task-specific workflow. Claude loads it on demand when the task matches its description, or you invoke it by name.
eg: Unlike an always-loaded instruction file, a skill's body costs almost nothing until it is used.

def: The YAML block at the top of SKILL.md that configures the skill: its name and description, who may invoke it, which tools it pre-approves, whether it runs in a forked context, and what argument hint to show.
eg: Unrecognized fields are ignored without an error, so a misspelled field name silently does nothing.

def: A skill setting that runs the skill in a separate subagent context that starts without the conversation history. Verbose output or exploratory work stays out of the main conversation, and only the result returns.
eg: It only helps skills that contain an explicit task. A skill that is just guidelines gives the subagent nothing to do.

def: A skill frontmatter field listing tools Claude may use without asking permission during the turn the skill runs, for example Bash(git commit *). It grants approval; it does not remove the tools that are not listed.
eg: The exam guide describes it as limiting what a skill can do. Current docs say it pre-approves; to take tools away use disallowed-tools, deny rules or a restricted agent type.

def: A skill frontmatter field holding a short hint such as [issue-number] that autocomplete shows, telling the developer which arguments the skill expects. Whatever the user types after the skill name reaches the body as $ARGUMENTS.
eg: It only prompts the user. It does not validate or require input.

def: A skill frontmatter setting that stops Claude from loading the skill on its own, so it runs only when a person types its name. It suits workflows with side effects, such as deploys or commits.
eg: Its counterpart, user-invocable set to false, hides a background-knowledge skill from the menu so only Claude can use it.

def: A copy of a team skill saved in the skills folder of your home directory under a different name, so you can adapt the workflow for yourself without changing what teammates get from the repository.
eg: Editing the committed project skill changes it for the whole team; a differently named personal copy changes nothing for anyone else.

def: The frontmatter text Claude reads to decide whether a skill fits the current task. Descriptions of available skills stay in context while the full body loads only on use, and long text is cut off, so the key use case should come first.
eg: A vague description makes a skill trigger at the wrong time or never.

def: The design choice between putting guidance in a skill, which loads only when a task needs it, and in the main instruction file, which is in context every session. Universal standards belong in the file; task-specific procedures belong in skills.
eg: Docs rule of thumb: when a section of the instruction file has grown into a multi-step procedure, make it a skill.

def: Where a skill lives decides who gets it: enterprise skills deployed by the organization, personal skills in the home directory, and project skills in the repository. When a name exists in several places, enterprise beats personal and personal beats project.
eg: Project skills are shared by committing them; personal ones never leave your machine.

def: A skill setting, used together with a forked context, that picks which subagent type executes the skill: a built-in such as the read-only Explore agent, or a custom one from .claude/agents/.
eg: The chosen agent type determines the model, tools and permissions of the forked run.

def: A rule file in .claude/rules/ whose YAML frontmatter lists glob patterns. Claude Code loads it only when Claude reads or edits a file that matches one of them, so conventions appear when relevant and stay out of context otherwise.
eg: It saves tokens and attention compared with putting every convention in one always-loaded file.

def: The only frontmatter key Claude Code reads in a rule file: a list, or a comma-separated string, of glob patterns that decide when the rule applies. A rule without it applies to everything.
eg: Example shape: paths set to a list holding "terraform/**/*". Malformed YAML is ignored and the rule loads unconditionally.

def: A rule whose patterns, such as one matching every test file name, follow a file type wherever those files sit in the tree, instead of being tied to one folder.
eg: This is the deciding advantage over directory-level instruction files, which only cover their own folder.

def: A rule file with no paths field. It loads at launch with the same priority as the main project instruction file and applies to all work in the session.
eg: Use it only for rules that really hold everywhere; otherwise add paths so the rule loads when it matters.

def: Path-scoped rules and nested instruction files enter the conversation when a matching file is touched, so summarizing the conversation folds them away; they load again the next time a matching file is read or edited.
eg: A rule that must survive compaction should be unconditional or live in the root instruction file, which is re-read from disk.

def: A Claude Code permission mode in which Claude reads files, runs exploratory commands and writes a proposed plan, but makes no source edits until you approve. You enter it with Shift+Tab, a /plan prefix or a startup flag.
eg: Built for large changes, several valid approaches and architectural decisions, where exploring first prevents costly rework.

def: Letting Claude make a change immediately, with no separate planning phase. It fits small, well-scoped work such as a single-file fix with a clear stack trace or one added validation check.
eg: Docs test: if you could describe the diff in one sentence, skip the plan.

def: A built-in, fast, read-only subagent for searching and analyzing a codebase in its own context window. The verbose discovery output stays there, and only a summary returns to the main conversation.
eg: It cannot write or edit files, and it starts without the project instruction files and git status to stay cheap.

def: Using plan mode to investigate and design, then approving the plan so the same session carries it out directly, for example planning a library migration and then performing it.
eg: The recommended phases are explore, plan, implement and commit. Each has its own best tool.

def: The point where Claude presents its plan and you choose how to proceed: approve with automatic edits, approve and review each edit yourself, or keep planning. You can open the plan in your editor and change it first.
eg: Approving exits the planning mode and switches the session to the permission mode you picked.

def: A session-level setting that decides which actions Claude can take without asking: default (manual), acceptEdits, plan, auto, dontAsk or bypassPermissions. Rules layered on top can allow, ask or deny specific tools.
eg: dontAsk denies anything not pre-approved, which suits locked-down CI; bypassPermissions belongs only in isolated containers or VMs.

def: How Claude Code evaluates allow, ask and deny rules: deny first, then ask, then allow, and the first match decides. A narrower allow rule cannot carve an exception out of a broader deny.
eg: That is why a broad deny always wins over a specific allow.

def: Automatic snapshots of file state taken before Claude's edits, letting you restore the conversation, the code or both to an earlier prompt. Only changes made through Claude's file-editing tools are tracked, not those made by shell commands.
eg: Not a replacement for git. It makes it cheap to try a risky approach and back out.

def: Two or three concrete before-and-after pairs that show an intended transformation, given when a prose description keeps being interpreted differently from run to run.
eg: Examples carry the format and the edge cases that words leave ambiguous.

def: Writing tests first for expected behavior, edge cases and performance, then letting Claude implement and iterate while you share the failing output after each attempt.
eg: A check Claude can run closes the loop: it keeps working until the tests pass instead of relying on you to spot mistakes.

def: Having Claude question you before it builds, about design considerations, edge cases and tradeoffs you may not have thought of, and then write a spec. It pays off in unfamiliar territory such as cache invalidation or failure modes.
eg: Docs suggest using the question tool for the interview, then starting a fresh session to execute the written spec.

def: A feedback guideline: when several problems interact, so that fixing one changes how another should be fixed, describe them together in one detailed message; when they are independent, fix them one after another.
eg: Sequential fixes of interacting bugs can undo each other.

def: A specific test case with sample input and expected output, such as a record containing a null value, given to Claude to fix one failing edge case instead of describing the problem abstractly.
eg: It pairs naturally with test-driven iteration.

def: The advice to clear the session and write a better opening prompt once you have corrected the same issue more than twice, because the context is by then cluttered with failed approaches.
eg: A clean session with a sharper prompt usually beats a long, patched one.

def: A check Claude can run to see whether its work is right, such as a test suite, a build exit code, a linter or a screenshot comparison, ideally written into the prompt together with example cases.
eg: Without one, "looks done" is the only signal and you become the verification loop.

def: Running Claude Code from a script by passing the prompt with the -p (print) flag: it processes the prompt, writes the result to standard output and exits without waiting for input. A non-zero exit code signals failure.
eg: Without it, a CI job can stall forever waiting for input that nobody will give.

def: A print-mode option that chooses text, json or stream-json output. The json form returns one object with the result text, session id and usage metadata that scripts can parse.
eg: stream-json emits newline-delimited events for real-time processing.

def: A print-mode option that takes a JSON Schema so the run's final answer comes back as validated structured data, found in the structured_output field of the JSON output.
eg: Use it together with json output to post machine-parseable findings, such as inline pull-request comments.

def: A startup option that skips automatic discovery of hooks, skills, plugins, MCP servers, auto memory and instruction files, so a scripted run behaves the same on every machine. Context is then supplied through flags.
eg: Recommended for CI in current docs. Because it also skips CLAUDE.md, pass needed guidance with an append-system-prompt flag.

def: A command-line option listing tools Claude may use without a permission prompt, written in rule syntax such as Bash(git diff *). It approves; it does not by itself restrict the other tools.
eg: In an unattended run pair it with dontAsk mode so everything else is denied rather than waiting for an answer.

def: A workflow action that runs Claude Code on GitHub events. With no prompt input it answers @claude mentions; with a prompt input it runs automatically, for example to review each pull request.
eg: Project standards come from the repository's CLAUDE.md, and the person who triggers a run needs write access.

def: Supplying the findings already posted on a pull request when a review reruns after new commits, and telling Claude to report only new or still-unaddressed issues, so developers do not see the same comment twice.
eg: The model has no memory of the earlier run. The pipeline must hand the earlier findings over.

def: Including the current test files in the prompt when generating tests in CI, so Claude can see which scenarios are already covered and avoid suggesting duplicates.
eg: Pair it with documented fixtures so new tests reuse what exists.

def: Documenting in the project instruction file the testing conventions, the criteria for a test worth writing and the available fixtures, so CI-invoked Claude Code generates focused tests and fewer low-value ones.
eg: This is how project context reaches a non-interactive run, provided the run does not skip instruction files.

def: A repository-root file of review-only instructions for Claude's code review: what counts as important versus a nit, how many nits to post, which paths to skip and what evidence a finding needs before it is posted.
eg: Unlike the main instruction file it is not applied to ordinary coding sessions.

def: A schema-defined list in which each finding carries a file, line, severity, description and suggested fix, so a script can post every entry as an inline pull-request comment.
eg: Free-text review output would need fragile parsing that breaks whenever the wording changes.

def: The failure in which an automated job stalls forever because Claude Code is waiting for input, such as a prompt or a permission dialog, that nobody can answer.
eg: Fix: run in print mode, and pre-approve or deny tools instead of prompting.

def: Specific, categorical rules that state which kinds of issues to report, such as bugs and security flaws, and which to skip, such as minor style or patterns that match local convention. They give the model a concrete decision boundary.
eg: Contrast with general instructions like "be conservative", which sound careful but do not change what gets flagged.

def: A vague request such as "be conservative" or "only report findings you are highly confident about". It sounds sensible but supplies no criterion, so false positives barely change.
eg: The fix is a categorical definition of what to report and what to skip, not a stronger tone.

def: The effect by which a review category that produces many wrong findings teaches developers to distrust, and then ignore, the accurate categories as well.
eg: Precision is an adoption problem as much as a metric: one noisy category can sink the whole tool.

def: Stopping a high-false-positive finding category from being posted while its prompt is improved, so developers keep trusting the categories that are accurate.
eg: Re-enable the category once its precision is acceptable. It is a trust-repair step, not a permanent removal.

def: Explicit definitions of each severity level, each paired with a concrete code example, so the same kind of defect receives the same label every time.
eg: Without examples, "critical" and "minor" drift between runs and between reviewers.

def: A narrowly defined test for raising a finding, such as flagging a docstring only when the behavior it claims conflicts with what the code actually does, instead of asking the model to check whether comments are good.
eg: A criterion the model can decide yes or no on gives far fewer false positives than a broad quality judgment.

def: Telling the model what to do rather than what to avoid, for example "write smoothly flowing prose paragraphs" instead of "do not use markdown".
eg: Docs list it among the most effective ways to steer output format.

def: Explaining why a constraint exists, for example that the text will be read aloud by a speech engine, so the model can generalize the rule to cases the instruction never mentioned.
eg: A bare "never do X" is followed literally; a reason lets the model apply the intent.

def: Wrapping instructions, context, examples and variable inputs in consistently named tags so the model can tell them apart. It reduces misreading in prompts that mix several kinds of content.
eg: Use the same tag names across prompts and nest tags where the content has a natural hierarchy, such as documents inside a documents tag.

def: Including a few worked input-and-output examples in the prompt to steer format, tone and judgment. It is the strongest remedy when detailed instructions alone give inconsistent results.
eg: Also called multishot prompting. Examples should be relevant, diverse and clearly delimited.

def: A few-shot example drawn from a borderline situation that shows which action was chosen and why it beat a plausible alternative.
eg: A handful of targeted examples of hard cases teach more than many easy ones.

def: An example whose main job is to show the exact shape of the output, such as location, issue, severity and suggested fix, so every response follows the same structure.
eg: Use it when the problem is inconsistent formatting rather than wrong judgment.

def: Few-shot examples that put code which is fine next to code that is truly wrong, each with a short reason, so the model learns the distinction and false positives fall without listing every allowed pattern.
eg: Examples teach the principle; a rule list only covers the cases it names.

def: The effect that a model shown well-chosen examples extends the underlying judgment to new patterns, instead of matching only the cases it has seen.
eg: It is why a few examples can outperform an exhaustive list of rules.

def: Examples taken from documents laid out differently, such as inline citations versus a bibliography, or a methods section versus details scattered through the text, so extraction works on every layout.
eg: Aim the set at the variety the real documents contain.

def: Adding examples that show the correct extraction from formats where a field kept coming back empty, because the model had not recognized where that information appears in them.
eg: It addresses missed values caused by layout, not values that are genuinely absent.

def: Wrapping each example in its own tag, and the whole set in an outer tag, so the model can distinguish examples from instructions. Good sets are relevant to the real task, diverse, and structured this way.
eg: Docs suggest roughly three to five examples for best results.

term: Extraction tool with a JSON schema
def: A tool whose input schema describes the data to extract. The model fills it in by calling the tool, and the application reads the structured result from the tool-use block's input instead of parsing free text.
eg: With strict tool use the input is guaranteed to match the schema; without it, validate in code.

def: An API option that supplies a JSON Schema in the output_config format setting so the model's reply itself is constrained to valid, schema-matching JSON, with no tool call required.
eg: Generally available. It complements strict tool use, which constrains tool inputs the same way.

def: The mechanism behind schema-guaranteed output: the schema is compiled into a grammar that limits which tokens the model may generate at each step.
eg: The first request with a new schema pays a compile delay; compiled grammars are cached for 24 hours.

def: A mistake that passes schema validation, for instance line items that do not add up to the stated total or a value placed in the wrong field. Constrained output removes syntax errors but cannot catch these.
eg: Catching them takes validation code and, where possible, cross-checks built into the schema.

def: The failure in which a field marked required makes the model supply a plausible value because the source document has none.
eg: Prevent it by making fields that may be absent optional or nullable.

def: A schema field that may be omitted or set to null when the document lacks the information, which lets the model report absence honestly instead of inventing a value.
eg: Reserve required fields for data that is always present.

def: A category field with a fixed list of values plus an "other" choice and a companion free-text field, so unexpected categories are captured without breaking the schema.
eg: It keeps the schema extensible without turning the field into unconstrained text.

def: An explicit option for cases where the source is ambiguous, so the model can say so rather than guess a specific category.
eg: Downstream code can route "unclear" items to review.

def: Prompt instructions telling the model how to standardize inconsistent source formatting, such as dates, currency and units, used alongside a strict output schema.
eg: The schema fixes the shape of the answer; the rules fix how messy values are turned into it.

def: Constraints on schemas for constrained output: objects must forbid extra properties, recursive schemas and numeric or string length limits are unsupported, and a request may carry only a limited number of strict tools and optional parameters.
eg: An unsupported feature produces a 400 error rather than silently loosening the schema.

def: The two cases in which constrained output may not match the schema: the model declines the request (stop reason refusal) or runs out of output tokens (stop reason max_tokens) and the result is incomplete.
eg: Always check the stop reason before trusting parsed output.

def: Checking model output against a typed Python model after extraction, so structural and business-rule violations become explicit errors that can drive a retry.
eg: Validation code complements schema-constrained output; it enforces rules the schema cannot express.

def: A retry whose request includes the original document, the failed extraction and the specific validation errors, so the model can correct exactly what was wrong instead of guessing.
eg: A bare "try again" repeats the same mistake. The error text is the useful signal.

def: A loop that validates each extraction in code, feeds any failures back with their errors, and retries a bounded number of times before routing the item to a human.
eg: The cap matters: some failures can never be fixed by retrying.

def: A failure that no retry can fix because the needed information is not in the supplied source, for example a value that exists only in an attachment that was never provided.
eg: Retries repair format and structure errors, not absent data.

def: A field in a structured finding that records which code construct triggered it, so dismissed findings can be grouped and their false-positive patterns analyzed.
eg: It turns developer dismissals into data for improving the criteria.

def: Studying which findings developers dismiss, using recorded triggers, to find systematic false positives and fix the criteria behind them.
eg: It closes the feedback loop between reviewers and the prompt.

def: A self-check design that extracts both the total printed in the document and the total computed from its line items, so a mismatch can be flagged for review.
eg: It catches semantic errors that schema validation cannot see.

def: A boolean in the output schema that the model sets when the source contains inconsistent data, making contradictions visible instead of silently resolved.
eg: Downstream code can send flagged records to review.

def: An asynchronous API for submitting many requests together at half the standard price. Processing may take up to 24 hours, though most batches finish much sooner, with no guaranteed latency; results are fetched after the batch ends.
eg: Cost savings in exchange for latency. It suits work nobody is waiting on.

def: Work where nobody is waiting for the answer, such as overnight reports, weekly audits and nightly test generation. It is the natural fit for asynchronous batch processing.
eg: Ask "does a person or a pipeline step block on this result?" If not, batch it.

def: A process that cannot continue until Claude's answer arrives, such as a pre-merge check a developer is waiting on. It needs the synchronous API because batch completion time is not guaranteed.
eg: The 50% saving does not justify an unbounded wait.

def: The identifier you attach to each request in a batch so every result can be matched to its request, because results are not guaranteed to come back in submission order.
eg: It is also how you find the failed items to resubmit.

def: Choosing how often to submit batches so that the worst-case wait for the next submission plus up to 24 hours of processing still meets a delivery deadline. For a 36-hour deadline, submissions can be at most 12 hours apart.
eg: Worst-case latency equals the submission interval plus the processing window.

def: After a batch ends, using custom_id to find only the failed or expired requests, fixing the cause (for example splitting an oversized document into chunks) and resubmitting just those.
eg: Never resubmit the whole batch for a handful of failures.

def: Tuning a prompt on a small representative sample before launching a large batch, so most requests succeed on the first pass and expensive resubmissions are avoided.
eg: Batch request parameters are validated asynchronously, so test the request shape with the synchronous API first.

def: The four outcomes reported per request when a batch ends: succeeded, errored, canceled and expired. Errored, canceled and expired requests are not billed.
eg: Handle each type: retry expired ones, fix and resubmit invalid-request errors.

term: No mid-request tool execution in batches
def: A batch request is a single asynchronous call, so the application cannot run a client-side tool, return its result and let the model continue within the same request.
eg: Tool-driven loops belong on the synchronous API. The guide states this as no multi-turn tool calling in a batch request.

def: Checking a batch's processing status until it reports that processing has ended, and only then retrieving results.
eg: You poll because a batch has no guaranteed completion time (most finish within an hour, the maximum is 24 hours), so check its status periodically instead of assuming it is done.

def: The tendency of a model to defend its own work when it reviews it in the same session, because it still holds the reasoning that produced the work.
eg: Telling the same session to be more critical does not remove the bias.

def: A second Claude session that sees only the code or diff and the review criteria, not the first session's reasoning, so it can question decisions the author would defend.
eg: More effective at catching subtle issues than self-review instructions or extended thinking in the same session.

def: Using one session to implement and a separate fresh session to review, then passing the reviewer's feedback back to the first session to address.
eg: A fresh context is not biased toward code it just wrote. Docs describe it for Claude Code workflows.

def: The point that giving the same session more reasoning time does not remove its bias toward its own earlier decisions; a separate instance without that context catches subtler issues.
eg: More thinking is not a second opinion.

def: A value the model attaches to each finding in a verification pass, used to route low-confidence findings to extra scrutiny. It is trustworthy for routing only after calibration against labeled data.
eg: Raw confidence numbers are a hint, not a measurement.

def: A fresh subagent asked to check a diff against criteria or to try to refute a result, so the agent that did the work is not the one grading it.
eg: Tell it to flag only gaps that affect correctness, or it may over-report to please the request.

def: The loss that occurs when repeated summaries squeeze exact figures, percentages, dates and customer-stated expectations into vague phrases like "a recent charge", leaving later steps without the facts they need.
eg: Each round of summarizing discards a little more precision; keep the exact facts somewhere that is never summarized.

def: A compact, persistent block of transactional facts such as amounts, dates, order numbers and statuses that is included in every prompt, kept apart from the summarized conversation history.
eg: It protects the numbers that matter from the drift of summarization.

def: The tendency of models to process the beginning and end of a long input more reliably than the middle, so findings buried in the middle sections may be left out of the answer.
eg: Mitigate by putting key material at the start or end and giving the rest clear section headers.

def: Placing a key-findings summary at the start of a large aggregated input and giving detailed sections explicit headers to counter position effects. For long documents, put the material first and the question last.
eg: Docs report better quality with the query at the end, especially for multi-document inputs.

def: Reducing a verbose tool result to the few fields that matter, for example five of forty fields on an order record, before it enters the conversation and keeps consuming tokens on every later turn.
eg: Tool results are the part of context that grows fastest and is least relevant afterwards.

def: The decline in accuracy and recall as more tokens accumulate in the window, which is why what you put in context matters as much as how much room is left.
eg: A bigger window does not cure it. Curating the contents does.

def: A separate store of structured data (order IDs, amounts, statuses) kept for each issue in a multi-issue session, so facts are not tangled together or lost as the conversation grows.
eg: Think of it as a ledger beside the chat transcript.

def: Having upstream agents return key facts, citations and relevance scores instead of long prose and reasoning chains, when the downstream agent has a limited context budget.
eg: Change the producer, not the consumer: verbose upstream output wastes the downstream window.

def: Dates, source locations and methodological context carried alongside findings in a subagent's structured output, so downstream synthesis can interpret and reconcile them correctly.
eg: Without it, numbers from different sources or periods cannot be compared fairly.

def: For long documents, asking the model to extract word-for-word quotes first and base its analysis on them, which focuses it on the relevant text and reduces unsupported claims.
eg: Docs recommend it for inputs over about twenty thousand tokens.

def: The situations that justify handing a case to a human: an explicit request for one, a policy exception or gap the agent cannot decide, and an inability to make meaningful progress. Mere complexity is not on the list.
eg: Make them explicit in the system prompt, with examples of escalating and of resolving.

def: Transferring right away when a customer explicitly asks for a person, without first trying to investigate or resolve the issue.
eg: Contrast with mere frustration, where offering a fix first is appropriate.

def: When a customer is upset but has not asked for a person and the issue is within the agent's ability, acknowledging the frustration and offering a resolution, escalating only if they repeat the wish for a human.
eg: It honors the customer without handing off cases the agent can fix.

def: Escalating when the written policy is ambiguous or silent about the specific request, for example a competitor price match when the policy covers only adjustments to the company's own prices.
eg: The agent should not improvise policy. A gap, not mere difficulty, is the trigger.

def: Triggering a handoff from detected customer emotion. Sentiment does not track how complex or risky a case is, so it sends easy cases to humans and keeps hard ones with the agent.
eg: An unreliable proxy for the thing that matters, which is whether the agent can resolve the case.

def: A number the model gives for how sure it is of its own answer. It is poorly calibrated, since the model is often confident on exactly the hard cases it gets wrong, so it is a weak basis for escalation.
eg: Confidence becomes usable only after calibration against labeled outcomes.

def: When a lookup returns several candidates, such as multiple customers with the same name, asking the user for an additional identifier instead of choosing by a heuristic like recency.
eg: Guessing the wrong account is worse than one more question.

def: Explicit rules in the system prompt for when to escalate and when to resolve, backed by worked examples of both, which fix unclear decision boundaries before heavier infrastructure is considered.
eg: The proportionate first fix when an agent escalates the wrong cases.

def: An error report that gives the failure type, the query or action attempted, any partial results and possible alternatives, so a coordinator can pick an informed recovery.
eg: It is what lets the coordinator choose between retrying, trying another source and continuing with what it has.

def: Returning an empty or default result as if the step succeeded when it actually failed, so nothing downstream knows anything went wrong.
eg: Worse than a visible failure: the coordinator reports a gap as if the topic had no findings.

def: Terminating an entire multi-step workflow because one step failed, discarding the work already done when recovery or partial results were possible.
eg: The opposite error to suppression. Both hide the useful middle path.

def: Notes in a synthesized report marking which findings are well supported and which topic areas have gaps because sources were unavailable.
eg: It lets readers trust the strong sections and see the weak ones.

def: Returning whatever a failed or interrupted subagent had gathered before it stopped, together with the error, so the coordinator can use it rather than starting over.
eg: Pair it with a note of what was attempted and what is missing.

def: The drift in a long exploratory session where answers become inconsistent and the model cites "typical patterns" instead of the specific classes it discovered earlier.
eg: Counter it with scratchpad notes, subagent delegation, summaries between phases and compaction.

def: A notes file in which an agent records key findings as it works and rereads for later questions, so facts survive context boundaries and compaction.
eg: Docs use the same idea for long tasks: structured state in JSON, free-form progress notes, and git history.

def: Handing specific questions, such as locating all test files or tracing a flow's dependencies, to subagents whose verbose output stays in their own context, while the main agent keeps the high-level picture.
eg: The main agent coordinates and receives summaries instead of raw search output.

def: Summarizing the findings of one exploration phase and placing that summary in the starting context of the agents that handle the next phase.
eg: It avoids both rediscovery and carrying the whole earlier transcript forward.

def: A file in a known location that records each agent's exported state, which the coordinator loads when resuming after a failure and injects into the agents' prompts.
eg: Without it, a crash in a long multi-agent run means starting over.

def: The Claude Code command that summarizes the conversation so far to free context while continuing the same session. Optional focus instructions steer what the summary keeps.
eg: Use it when discovery output has filled the window; it differs from clearing, which discards the conversation.

def: Claude Code's behavior of summarizing older conversation when the window nears its limit. The project-root instruction file is re-read from disk afterward, while instructions given only in chat can be lost.
eg: Put anything that must persist in the instruction file, not in a one-off message.

def: The Claude Code command that starts a fresh conversation with empty context, used between unrelated tasks or after repeated failed corrections.
eg: It resets rather than summarizes, so carry over anything you still need.

def: An API feature in which Claude summarizes earlier turns on the server so a long conversation can continue past the context limit without custom summarization code.
eg: Currently in beta, available in on-demand and token-threshold forms.

def: A context-editing strategy that removes the oldest tool results once the conversation passes a threshold, leaving placeholders, so agentic workflows do not drown in stale output.
eg: Works by rule rather than by summarizing. Clearing invalidates cached prefixes, so clear enough to be worth it.

def: A client-side tool through which Claude reads and writes files in a /memories directory that the application implements, giving agents persistence across context windows and sessions.
eg: Claude requests the file operations and your code executes them against storage you control.

def: The way an overall accuracy figure, such as 97 percent, can hide poor results on particular document types or fields.
eg: Always break accuracy down by segment before reducing human review.

def: Drawing random samples separately from each segment, such as document type or confidence band, to measure error rates and spot new failure patterns, including among high-confidence extractions.
eg: It keeps checking the outputs that automation would otherwise stop checking.

def: A per-field value the model reports for each extracted item, used to decide which fields need human review once the thresholds have been calibrated.
eg: Finer-grained than a score per document, so reviewers see only the doubtful fields.

def: Checking model-reported confidence against a labeled validation set and setting review thresholds from the accuracy actually observed at each confidence level.
eg: Uncalibrated scores mislead. A 0.9 should mean roughly nine in ten are right.

def: Measuring accuracy separately by document type and by field before reducing human review, to confirm that performance is consistent in every segment.
eg: Automate a segment only after it passes on its own.

def: Sending extractions with low confidence, or with ambiguous or contradictory sources, to human reviewers first, so limited review capacity goes where errors are likeliest.
eg: Combine it with random sampling of the confident ones.

def: A structured record linking each claim to its source URL or document name and a supporting excerpt, preserved and merged as findings pass through summarization and synthesis.
eg: It is what makes a synthesized report auditable.

def: The disappearance of where a claim came from when findings are compressed into summaries without carrying their source mappings along.
eg: Prose summaries are where citations quietly vanish.

def: Keeping both values when credible sources disagree and labeling each with its source, rather than silently choosing one.
eg: Let the reader or coordinator reconcile with the evidence in view.

def: Requiring publication or data-collection dates in structured outputs so that numbers from different times are not mistaken for contradictions.
eg: A statistic that changed between 2021 and 2025 may be a trend, not a conflict.

def: A report layout that separates well-established findings from disputed ones while keeping the original sources' characterizations and methods.
eg: Readers can see at a glance where confidence is high.

def: Presenting synthesized material in the form that suits it, such as financial data in tables, news as prose and technical findings as structured lists, instead of one uniform format.
eg: Forcing everything into bullets destroys information.

def: A design in which a document-analysis agent returns conflicting values explicitly annotated and the coordinator decides how to reconcile them before synthesis.
eg: The analysis agent reports; the coordinator, which sees the whole task, decides.
